title: IFAK at 62: Celebrating St John Bosco's Day with a Commitment to Inclusive Boarding
author: Cedric NIYONKURU
imageAlt: IFAK students, parents and alumni gathered for Holy Mass during the 62nd anniversary celebration in school chapel
description: On 7 February 2026, the IFAK community celebrated the Feast of St John Bosco while marking 62 years of the institution's contribution to education — and heard a heartfelt call for a girls' dormitory.
content:
On 7 February, the IFAK community celebrated the Feast of St John Bosco while marking 62 years of the institution's contribution to education in Rwanda. Beyond the celebration, the day highlighted a shared call for greater inclusion, particularly the need for a girls' dormitory.

The celebration began with a Holy Mass, bringing together students, teachers, alumni, parents and friends in a spirit inspired by the values of St John Bosco.

Speaking on behalf of the students, Head Boy Mukyo Thadee expressed gratitude for the school's guidance and education. “We are deeply thankful for the quality education and the loving guidance we receive at IFAK,” he said. “The Salesian values of St John Bosco continue to inspire us every day.”

The defining moment of the celebration came from Head Girl Isimbi Ellah, who addressed a long-standing concern. “The absence of a girls' dormitory limits our full participation in boarding life,” she explained. “We want to feel fully included, sharing the same experiences as our brothers. This is not just a wish — it is a step toward equality and unity in our school.” Her words were met with applause and strong support from the audience.

Following the students, alumni representative Mr. Nkuranga Alphonse, who studied at IFAK in 1989, echoed their appeal. “From its earliest days, IFAK has welcomed change and growth,” he said. “Opening boarding for girls will strengthen unity and joy among all students, just as the school has always embraced progress.”

A parent representative also praised the school's commitment to education and values. “We appreciate how IFAK instills the Salesian values in our children, which align with Rwanda's vision of forming good citizens,” she said. “We strongly support the call for a girls' dormitory, as it will allow our children to grow together and strengthen family unity.”

The Director of IFAK, Rev. Fr. Ntirenganya Jean Bosco, responded to these concerns. “We hear the strong desire to host both boys and girls in boarding,” he said. “Plans for a girls' dormitory are included in our future development projects, along with a football pitch and a gymnasium. Our goal is to provide a complete environment for education and growth.”

The institution traces its origins to Collège Notre Dame, founded in 1962 as a carpentry and mechanical workshop school. It later gained private school status in 1988 and became the Institut de Formation Apostolique de Kimihurura (IFAK), continuing a legacy of quality education and inclusion. The school has been operating since 1964, celebrated its golden jubilee in 2015, and in 2026 marked 62 years of Salesian education and evangelisation in Kimihurura, Gasabo, Kigali.
source: Adapted from the official IFAK website (ifakdonbosco.ac.rw). Photo: official IFAK website.

title: Barore Reflects on the Values He Gained from IFAK That Shaped His Life and Career
author: Cedric NIYONKURU
imageAlt: IFAK alumni gathering in the school courtyard during the 62nd anniversary celebration
description: Cleophas Barore, Director General of the Rwanda Broadcasting Agency, reflects on the discipline, humility and lifelong learning he gained as a student at IFAK between 1985 and 1991.
content:
As IFAK Don Bosco Kimihurura celebrated the feast of St John Bosco and its 62nd anniversary of providing education in Rwanda, Cleophas Barore, Director General of the Rwanda Broadcasting Agency (RBA), reflected on his educational journey at the school and the values he says became pillars of both his life and professional career.

Barore studied at IFAK Don Bosco Kimihurura from 1985 to 1991, where he received knowledge and moral education that, according to him, have never left him and which he still considers a unique legacy.

“On this 62nd anniversary, it is a joy to be together with the school's leadership, teachers and alumni, thanking God — and also acknowledging the priest through whom God worked, Don Bosco — by instilling in him a heart that loved young people and cared for children's well-being, especially those from underprivileged families,” he said.

He particularly recalled a unique tradition at IFAK Don Bosco, where students were given a daily word of wisdom known as “le mot du soir.” The tradition has since expanded to “le mot du matin” to include day scholars, while “le mot du soir” continues for boarding students. “That daily word was something you could never forget. Knowing that this tradition continues — that students are still given words of wisdom and advice every day — is something every former IFAK student deeply misses,” he said.

Barore also spoke about the Salesian approach to education, based on closeness to children, where educators shared daily life with students. “We played football with priests and brothers. There was a strong sense of fraternity, and they reminded us that even if we did not continue on the path of religious life, at the very least we should become citizens who are useful to the country.”

Among the values he says he gained from IFAK are humility, discipline and a commitment to lifelong learning. He added that even the punishments students received were intended to build them, as punishment was used as a form of teaching. “If you were late, the punishment was to read a book and later present a summary of it. You were punished, but you left having gained knowledge. It was a form of corrective discipline,” he said.

He believes today's IFAK students are fortunate, as the school continues to uphold Don Bosco's vision of educating a well-rounded person who contributes to both the Church and the nation. “We heard a priest say: we are still pursuing Don Bosco's dream. I think that if you pay attention and follow carefully, no child can leave IFAK with an empty mind,” he said.

To today's students aspiring to the heights reached by people they admire, Barore's message was clear: “Today's world shows you where people have reached, but not the path they took to get there. If you want to be like someone you admire, you must first understand what it required of them. It requires hard work, higher standards of behavior, patience and consistency. Knowledge without good values is meaningless.”

Cleophas Barore has been Director General of the Rwanda Broadcasting Agency since 2023. He began his journalism career at ORINFOR in 1995 and served as Chairperson of the Rwanda Media Commission from December 2016 until November 2024.
source: Adapted from the official IFAK website (ifakdonbosco.ac.rw). Photo: official IFAK website.

title: IFAK Shines as First Runner-Up in Money Makeover Challenge Cohort 3
author: NIYOMUNGERI Cyprien
imageAlt: IFAK students presenting their financial project to a panel of judges at the Money Makeover Challenge final
description: Institut de Formation Apostolique de Kimihurura secured the First Runner-Up position in the Money Makeover Challenge Cohort 3, organised by the Bank of Kigali with iDebate Rwanda.
content:
In a remarkable display of financial literacy and innovation, Institut de Formation Apostolique de Kimihurura (IFAK) secured the First Runner-Up position in the Money Makeover Challenge Cohort 3, an initiative organised by the Bank of Kigali in partnership with iDebate Rwanda.

The Money Makeover Challenge is a dynamic financial literacy competition designed to equip secondary school students with essential money-management skills. Through mentorship provided by professionals from the Bank of Kigali, students learn to apply financial knowledge to real-world scenarios, developing practical business plans based on case studies designed by the bank itself.

Top-performing students from participating schools formed teams of three to represent their institutions in the final rounds. These teams presented innovative and realistic financial projects before a panel of judges, showcasing viable business ideas, sustainable budgeting, economic impact and transformative potential.

The competition saw participation from some of Rwanda's leading schools, including College St. André, Riviera High School, ESSA Nyarugunga, Kagarama Secondary School, Lycée Notre Dame de Cîteaux and École Ste. Bernadette Kamonyi, among others.

Representing IFAK with excellence, the team composed of Balinda Cyemezo Bruce, Ineza Eluine and Kamanzi Marvel Frank demonstrated commendable skill and creativity in their financial project. Their efforts earned them the runner-up position, just behind Kagarama Secondary School, which claimed the top spot with their outstanding project.

As part of the prize, IFAK's team received 450,000 Rwandan Francs, directly deposited into their individual accounts at the Bank of Kigali. The reward is intended to support the implementation of their proposed project or to fund any other initiatives that contribute to financial empowerment and life transformation.

The Money Makeover Challenge continues to play a significant role in nurturing a financially savvy generation — promoting innovation, entrepreneurship and responsible money management among Rwanda's youth. Congratulations to Team IFAK.
source: Adapted from the official IFAK website (ifakdonbosco.ac.rw). Photo: official IFAK website.

title: Kwibuka31: Amb. Nsengimana Urges IFAK Students to Embrace Love and Unity
author: NIYOMUNGERI Cyprien
imageAlt: IFAK students and staff standing in silence during the Kwibuka31 commemoration ceremony
description: On 30 May 2025, IFAK students gathered to commemorate the 31st anniversary of the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi, in a ceremony attended by Ambassador and Senator Joseph Nsengimana.
content:
On Friday, 30 May 2025, students of the Institut de Formation Apostolique de Kimihurura (IFAK) gathered to commemorate the 31st anniversary of the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda. During the event, they were urged to draw lessons from the country's dark past to help build a better future anchored in love and unity.

The event paid tribute to former IFAK educators, students, staff and others who were killed during the genocide. A wreath was laid at a memorial site bearing the names of those who perished, whose remains now rest with dignity at the Kigali Genocide Memorial in Gisozi.

Speaking at the event, IFAK Principal Father Jean Bosco Ntirenganya emphasised that remembering the victims of the genocide is both a responsibility and a debt owed to them by all Rwandans. He highlighted that schools have a vital role in teaching young people to resist genocide ideology and prevent the recurrence of such atrocities.

“Commemoration is a time to educate the youth about the history of the Genocide against the Tutsi. It helps us guard against anything that could bring back that tragic history and to denounce genocide ideology, wherever it may appear — within or beyond our borders,” said Fr. Ntirenganya.

Alphonse Nsengimana, representing IBUKA (the umbrella organisation for Genocide survivors), praised IFAK for organising the memorial, describing it as an effective approach to confronting those who deny or downplay the genocide. He stressed the importance of educating the younger generation to reject denialism and champion truth. He traced Rwanda's painful history back to colonial rule, particularly the Belgian administration, which laid the foundations of ethnic divisions that eventually culminated in the genocide, and paid tribute to the Rwandan Patriotic Army, who halted the genocide and liberated the country.

Ambassador and Senator Joseph Nsengimana, the guest of honour, is an IFAK alumnus and one of its earliest students. He recounted how he ended up at IFAK due to discriminatory practices during the pre-genocide era that denied Tutsi access to education. He focused his message on the moral lessons depicted in plays performed by the young students, which illustrated kindness overcoming evil and the power of love as a legacy worth passing on.

“Good always triumphs over evil — but building goodness takes time and effort. The most valuable legacy we can leave is one of love, real love that is free from hatred,” he said. “Today's world shows where people have reached — but not the path they took to get there,” he added, urging the youth to cultivate values rooted in compassion and unity.

More than 85 people known to have been killed at IFAK during the genocide — including teachers, students and civilians who had sought refuge there — were remembered during the ceremony, which took place during Rwanda's official 100-day commemoration period honouring over a million victims of the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi.
source: Adapted from the official IFAK website (ifakdonbosco.ac.rw). Photo: official IFAK website.

title: Kimihurura Parish: ADMA Vows with Deep Devotion
author: IFAK Communications
imageAlt: Mass during the ADMA profession of vows at Mary Help of Christians Parish, Kimihurura, May 2025
description: On 25 May 2025, Mary Help of Christians Parish celebrated its annual feast with a solemn Mass led by Bishop Casimir Uwumukiza and the first profession of vows by 25 ADMA members, in communion with the IFAK Don Bosco community.
content:
On 25 May 2025, Mary Help of Christians Parish in Kimihurura — the parish of the IFAK Don Bosco community — joyfully celebrated its annual feast day with a vibrant and spiritually enriching ceremony.

The celebration was highlighted by a solemn Holy Mass led by Bishop Casimir Uwumukiza, Auxiliary Bishop of the Archdiocese of Kigali, and attended by parishioners, clergy and members of the Salesian Family.

A central moment was the first profession of vows by 25 members of the Association of Mary Help of Christians (ADMA) — a lay movement rooted in Marian spirituality, founded by St John Bosco in 1869. Among those professing, 22 were from Kimihurura and 3 from the Diocese of Kabgayi, who renewed their vows. The ceremony was presided over by Fr. Gabriel Ngendakuriyo, Salesian Provincial for Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi.

Speaking on behalf of his fellow members during the reception, a representative of ADMA-Kimihurura expressed deep gratitude to God, their mentors and parish leaders — especially thanking Fr. Gabriel and Fr. Jean Bosco Ntirenganya for their support. Fr. Gabriel emphasised the importance of devotion to Mary Help of Christians in today's world, highlighting her role in fostering peace, unity and faith: “We must continue to share and teach the love we have for Mary to others. The world needs a Mother like Mary to grow in unity, peace and faith.”

ADMA, open to all lay faithful, promotes daily prayer, sacramental life and active charity. Its growing presence in Kimihurura reflects the parish's dynamic spiritual life under Salesian leadership — a parish of nearly 3,000 Catholics and a stronghold of faith, love and service.

IFAK is a Catholic school of the Salesians of Don Bosco. The charism of St John Bosco — a loving, educating and evangelising presence among the young — animates both school life and parish life, and celebrations such as the feast of Mary Help of Christians are a natural meeting point for the two. The IFAK community congratulates the parish and its new ADMA members.
source: Adapted from the official IFAK website (ifakdonbosco.ac.rw). Photo: official IFAK website.

title: Students at IFAK Begin Weekly Tests to Prepare for the National Examinations
author: NIZEYIMANA Jean de Dieu
imageAlt: Senior Three and Senior Six students at IFAK writing a silent national-style examination paper
description: Ordinary Level finalists and Advanced Level students at IFAK have begun structured weekly tests to sharpen their preparation for the national examinations.
content:
The Ordinary Level finalists (O' Level) at IFAK began weekly tests with the aim of sharpening their skills and abilities in preparing for the national examinations efficiently.

The Dean of Studies at IFAK, Isaïe Mwizerwa, explained that teachers prepare weekly tests for students of Senior Three and Senior Six in order to help them become familiar with the national exams. The tests are done every Monday and Friday for Senior Three students, and on Monday for Senior Six students.

Mwizerwa emphasises that the tests are set as the National Exams are, with teachers referring to the topics taught over the three years of the level — for Senior Three, the tests cover all the necessary topics from Senior One. “This helps students become familiar with the national exams and the time for doing those exams (three hours). Because those tests are set referring to the national exams, the students get abilities to succeed,” he said.

The marks of the tests are recorded on the school report. Since last year, the marks have been proclaimed alone and arranged accordingly. “After starting these tests, the results are positive, especially for last year, and we hope this year and the following years will be better,” Mwizerwa added.

IFAK is a private secondary school located at Kimihurura sector, Gasabo District, in the City of Kigali. The school belongs to the Salesians of Don Bosco, a religious congregation and Catholic Church faith-based organisation recognised and registered as a legal entity as “Oeuvres de Don Bosco au Rwanda.”

The school has both Ordinary Level and Advanced Level. In Advanced Level, IFAK offers five combinations: PCM (Physics–Chemistry–Mathematics), MCB (Mathematics–Chemistry–Biology), MCE (Mathematics–Computer Science–Economics), MEG (Mathematics–Economics–Geography) and MPC (Mathematics–Physics–Computer Science).
source: Adapted from the official IFAK website (ifakdonbosco.ac.rw). Photo: official IFAK website.
